active_narratives.title: Hyperscaler AI Capex Bubble Concerns: Datacenter $1.7T by 2030 vs. ROI Validation Risk
active_narratives.summary: Hyperscaler AI capex is running far ahead of the original $1.7T-by-2030 framing: the Big Four alone guide to roughly $735B in 2026 (Alphabet $195-205B, Amazon ~$220B after raising from ~$200B on Jul 30, Microsoft $175B restated from ~$190B on a useful-life reclass with spend unchanged, Meta $135-145B after raising the floor $10B on Jul 29) and analysts project ~$1T in 2027. Semiconductor supply chains benefit directly, but ROI-validation and financing-cost concerns have intensified as the numbers grew.
active_narratives.thesis: AI infrastructure spending remains a strong tailwind for semis, memory, optics and power infrastructure, but multiple-compression risk emerges if capex growth decelerates or demand does not materialise. The Q2 2026 print season is now COMPLETE and it resolved in favour of continuation: all four reported by 30 July and none guided down — Alphabet RAISED to $195-205B on 22 July flagging a significant further increase in 2027, Meta raised its floor to $135-145B on 29 July, Microsoft restated to $175B on a useful-life reclass with spend unchanged, and Amazon RAISED to ~$220B on 30 July. Read the Amazon raise as a different kind: it was attributed to HIGHER MEMORY COSTS — paying more for the same capacity, not buying more — so it is a weaker demand signal than a unit-driven raise and it transmits to memory vendors rather than along the whole chain, though Jassy said Amazon still will not have enough capacity for 2026 demand. The live constraint has shifted from willingness to spend toward the cost of funding it — Meta's $12B El Paso datacenter bond priced above its record 2025 deal and Amazon's $25B July issue drew about half the order book of its March deal. Rates compound this: the Fed is priced hold-versus-hike rather than easing, which is a duration headwind for capex-intensive mega-caps. A first guide-down or 'digestion' framing from any major hyperscaler would be a cluster-wide thesis-break check, not a single-ticker event.

active_narratives.title: US-China Semiconductor Supply Chain Reshaping: Tariffs vs. Foundry Demand
active_narratives.summary: US-China technology restrictions continue to reshape semiconductor supply chains, but the direction is now mixed rather than uniformly escalating. ASML's standing 2030 ambition is EUR 44-60B revenue set at its Nov 2024 Investor Day and never revised, and Intel's 18A is in volume production with High-NA EUV in high-volume manufacturing. Onshoring economics support equipment and memory capex, while China's materials levers (helium prohibition in force; rare-earth and Ga/Ge suspensions lapsing 10 and 27 November 2026) are the retaliation channel.
active_narratives.thesis: Structural supply-chain tailwinds from US-China decoupling support the onshoring complex — Intel 18A and 14A, ASML EUV, Micron's ~$250B cumulative US plan through 2035 — while elevated cost of capital constrains the multiple paid for that demand. The July 2026 policy picture is genuinely two-directional: Treasury sanction threats and an open-model distillation probe are officials speaking rather than agencies acting, with no designation or docket, while the Hong Kong emergency order was allowed to lapse on 14 July and MOFCOM is consulting on reciprocal tariff cuts covering roughly $30B each way. The durable read is that rhetoric moves faster than rules: weight enacted measures (the helium prohibition, the November materials cliffs, existing licence regimes) over statements. On H200 exports to China the binding constraint is Beijing, not Washington — licences exist on both sides but realised volume is negligible.

active_narratives.title: ECB Rate Hold Diverges from Fed Hawkish Pause: Euro Weakness Implication
active_narratives.summary: ECB held the deposit rate at 2.25% on Jul 23, 2026 after hiking 25bp on Jun 11 — its first hike since 2023 — with markets pricing a hike at the Sep 10 projection meeting. The divergence has INVERTED: this is a tightening bias, not an easing cycle, and with the Fed priced hold-versus-hike the two are converging rather than diverging. DXY 101.48 still reflects a US rate premium.
active_narratives.thesis: The ECB is in a tightening bias, not an easing one: 25bp on Jun 11 to a 2.25% deposit rate, held unanimously on Jul 23 with some governors questioning whether more was warranted. July was a non-projection meeting so the bar to move was structurally higher; Sep 10 carries fresh forecasts and is the live decision. Energy-driven inflation is the shared driver with the Fed, so the policy gap is NARROWING — the euro-weakness-on-divergence leg is the part of this narrative most at risk of being wrong. Eurozone business activity has returned to growth, which removes the 'subdued growth forces easing' premise the original thesis rested on. Global duration headwinds across developed markets still hold as a conclusion, but now because everyone is tightening, not because the Fed is an outlier.

active_narratives.title: US-Iran Hormuz Blockade Escalation: Oil Supply Crisis Resurfaces
active_narratives.summary: US naval blockade of Iranian ports and the Hormuz disruption are INTACT: as of Jul 21, 2026 the Persian Gulf Strait Authority stated passage through the strait 'is currently not possible', non-Iranian-linked transits fell to 25 from 108 week-on-week and total traffic is down roughly 90% year-on-year, with no ceasefire or negotiated settlement. What has collapsed is the PRICE premium, not the disruption -- WTI peaked at $104.91 in April and sits at $81.54 on Jul 28, -22%, after a US-Iran strike pause around Jul 26-27. Logistics disruption (airspace closures, shipping reroutes) persists.
active_narratives.thesis: The load-bearing tension is that physical disruption and the oil premium have DECOUPLED. Do not read falling crude as the strait reopening, and do not read the blockade as a standing bid under oil: Hormuz passage remains blocked and the blockade is in force, yet WTI fell from $104.91 to $81.54 because the strike pause removed escalation risk, not because supply was restored. Transmission legs that still apply: logistics cost inflation from rerouting and tanker diversions pressures semiconductor supply chains (ASML, TSM, MU). The leg that has REVERSED is the inflation/rate one -- July FOMC hike odds that the oil spike drove up to ~38% fell back to roughly one-in-three as crude retreated, and the hike risk migrated to the Sep 10 meeting rather than disappearing. Falsifiable both ways: resumed strikes re-arm the premium, while an actual reopening of the strait would be the first genuine supply improvement and has NOT happened.

active_narratives.title: Microsoft Azure AI Revenue Concentration: OpenAI 45% Backlog Dependency
active_narratives.summary: Microsoft's disclosed 45% OpenAI share of Azure backlog is a DECEMBER-quarter figure that has never been refreshed — do not quote it as current. The commercial agreement was rewritten in late April 2026: cloud exclusivity ended and the AGM clause was eliminated, so OpenAI can now buy compute elsewhere. Q4 FY2026 printed Jul 29, 2026: commercial RPO $678B (+84% YoY) and Azure +43% constant currency, both ahead of the prior $627B/~40%.
active_narratives.thesis: Single-vendor concentration risk is real but has moved on two axes since this was written. The late-April rewrite ended cloud exclusivity, so the forward question is no longer lock-in but whether OpenAI-linked Azure consumption DECELERATES now that it can buy elsewhere — the cleaner read on calls is Azure growth ex-OpenAI, since credit-funded OpenAI consumption is not external customer demand. Microsoft is also actively reducing the dependency, launching in-house models it says cut costs up to 89% versus OpenAI. Capex is the swing factor: $175B restated for 2026 (from ~$190B — a useful-life reclass, spend unchanged, NOT a cut), with memory prices as the cost driver — a direct link to the memory-supercycle narrative, now confirmed from outside Microsoft by Amazon naming higher memory costs as the reason for its ~$200B to ~$220B raise on Jul 30. Two anchors here are stale and should not be reused: the 45% backlog share (December quarter, never refreshed) and the $1.7T-by-2030 capex figure, against Big-4 2026 guided capex of roughly $735B. US10Y is 4.64%, not 4.42%.

active_narratives.title: BigTech AI Strategy Divergence: GOOG TPU Upgrade vs MSFT/AMZN Caution
active_narratives.summary: Market differentiating BigTech AI exposure by structure rather than by any single day's rating: GOOG's in-house TPU stack, MSFT's OpenAI/Azure concentration, AMZN's capex load. Signal states across the three have churned repeatedly -- GOOG ran BUY to CAUTION to HOLD between June and late July -- so the durable content here is the structural split, not a signal triple that decays within days.
active_narratives.thesis: Divergence reflects structural AI strategy differences. GOOG benefits from owning its accelerator roadmap -- Ironwood GA, with 8th-gen Sunfish/Zebrafish only in select-customer preview and GA not until late 2027 -- and raised FY26 capex to $195-205B (NOT the '>=$180B' an earlier update recorded: $180-190B was the PRIOR guide). MSFT's OpenAI concentration is the most-cited risk but has softened -- the late-April rewrite ended cloud exclusivity and MSFT is shipping in-house models it says cut costs up to 89% -- and the 45% Azure-backlog share is a December-quarter figure never refreshed, so it should not be quoted as current. AMZN carries ~$220B FY26 capex (raised from ~$200B on 30 July, attributed to higher memory costs) against a genuine AWS reacceleration -- Q2 AWS grew 37% to $42.2B, its fastest since Q4 2021. The Jul 22-30 print window has now CLOSED and all three reported, so the June framing is superseded: the actuals show all three still raising or holding capex with none guiding down, and the divergence now runs on who funds it from operating cash and who is paying input-cost inflation for the same capacity.
